title: Reply of the Chief Electoral Officer, Maharashtra, to The Reporters’ Collective
shows: This letter concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In a four-page letter to the Reporters' Collective dated 20 November and posted on X on 22 November, signed by M.R. Parkar, Joint Secretary and Joint Chief Electoral Officer, the office of Maharashtra's Chief Electoral Officer says the Collective's report is based on factual inaccuracies and calls its title completely misleading. It says that at the Assembly election of 2024 the returning officers entered the polling percentage every two hours in the Commission's Encore software from the start of the poll, that citizens could see it on the Voter Turnout app for each slot from 7 am to 5 pm, and that after this an approximate percentage at the close of poll was made available and finally what it calls the accurate percentage, collected from the presiding officers, was published on the same app. It says the hours of poll were 7 am to 6 pm in 285 of the 288 Assembly seats and were cut to 3 pm in three seats of Gadchiroli district, and on its third page it gives the hours of 7 am to 6 pm for 283 of the 288. It describes the returning officer's report in Annexure 44 as an administrative narrative of 48 points written by hand and a non-statutory summary, and says the figures in the Commission's index cards trace back to Form 17C. It says the Collective's statement that officials kept no record of voting between 5 pm and 6 pm in 114 Assembly seats rests on point 42 of that report, which asks only for the votes cast every two hours up to 5 pm and the slips issued at the close of poll, and that the votes cast after 5 pm in any seat can be worked out by subtracting the votes at 5 pm from the total recorded at point 18. It says the number of slips handed to voters in the queue at the close of poll is recorded in the presiding officer's diary, which it calls a statutory document. It gives the turnout at the Assembly election of 2024 as 58.22% at 5 pm and 66.05% at the end of poll, a difference of 7.83, against 6.67 at the Assembly election of 2019 and between 8.23 and 10.15 in the five phases of the Lok Sabha election of 2024 in the state, and says the voting shows no surge after 5 pm. It says the Collective emailed its questions on 16 November at 10.03 am and asked for a reply by 5 pm the same day.
quote: First of all, title claiming “the ECI has no record of How Many Citizens voted after 5.00 pm in 2024 elections” is completely misleading.
One can easily calculate votes cast after 5.00 pm in any constituency by subtracting votes cast at 5.00 pm from total votes casted.
note: First reading, 23 November 2026. The post of 22 November 2026 at 16:21 UTC (9:51 pm IST) by the account ChiefElectoralOffice (@CEO_Maharashtra), read through api.fxtwitter.com on 23 November 2026, and its four attached pages (pbs.twimg.com/media/HXvgm3IaIAASMYC, HXvgnkSbgAAh-Dz, HXvgoWwbYAAkjD6 and HXvgpGSbwAAM5j6) read as images, in the order posted, numbered 1 to 4. The post's text reads 'Reply of the Chief Electoral Officer, Maharashtra, to The Reporters’ Collective regarding Its Report Titled “Part 2: Election Audit – In 200 Seats, the ECI Has No Record of How Many Citizens Voted After 5:00 PM in the 2024 Elections” @reporters_co', and the title here is its words up to The Reporters’ Collective. The letter is No. CEL-2026/C.R. 190/26//E-1 of the Office of Chief Electoral Officer, Maharashtra State, dated 20.11.2026, addressed to The Reporters' Collective, and signed by M.R. Parkar, Joint Secretary and Joint Chief Electoral Officer, Maharashtra State. Both quotes are verbatim, the first from page 1 and the second from page 3. The letter is inconsistent with itself on the hours of poll. Page 1 reads '7.00 am to 6.00 pm in 285 out of 288 ACs. Only in 3 ACs of Gadchiroli district, said period was curtailed to 3.00 pm', and page 3 reads '07.00 am to 06.00 pm for 283 out of 288 Assembly Constituencies'. Both are given as printed and the summary does not say which is right. The paragraph on Annexure 44 is printed twice, on page 3 and again on page 4. The table on page 4 gives, for the 5 pm figure, the end of poll and the difference, MLA 2019 54.43, 61.10 and 6.67, Lok Sabha 2024 Phase I 54.85, 63.71 and 8.86, Phase II 53.51, 62.71 and 9.2, Phase III 53.40, 63.55 and 10.15, Phase IV 52.49, 62.21 and 9.72, Phase V 48.66, 56.89 and 8.23, and MLA 2024 58.22, 66.05 and 7.83. Every difference equals the end-of-poll figure less the 5 pm figure. The letter says the 2024 Assembly figure at 5 pm is approximate, recorded on Encore, and the end-of-poll figure is as recorded in 17-C. The no-surge sentence is the letter's reading of its own chart of the Assembly poll of 2024. Not carried are the letter's challenge to name the experts the report cites on bogus voting in the last hour, its account of the Kopri-Pachpakhadi seat, which names two parties' candidates, its statement that two-hourly figures pass from presiding officer to returning officer by telephone, and its remark that the elections were held three years ago. Part 2 of the Collective's series is in round 50, with the Haryana reply of 18 November, and that note records that Maharashtra's reply of 18 November, a card with six points, was seen only as a screenshot. This letter of 20 November is a separate and longer reply. It concerns the 2024 polls, so nothing in it can be checked against the site's roll data, and every figure is the office's.

title: Explainer: Can the SIR Be Rectified?
shows: Rangarajan R., a former IAS officer, sets out the Supreme Court's judgment of May 2026 upholding the revision in Bihar and asks whether the revision can be put right. In his summary the court held that the Commission may revise the roll for many or all constituencies of a state under section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act read with Article 324, that the measures are proportionate and keep the safeguards of notice and hearing, and that the Commission may make a limited enquiry into citizenship for the purpose of the roll, with any deletion on grounds of citizenship referred to the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, 1955. He sets the revision beside the Commission's guidelines of May 2002 for the last intensive revision, under which supervisors were to check at least 25% of the households at random, electors who had moved were enrolled at their new address in the same exercise, and claims and objections filed in bulk were to be rejected summarily. In the present revision, he writes, the notification issued before Bihar's revision asks supervisors for 10% random verification, an elector marked shifted has to apply on Form 8 at the new address or afresh on Form 6, and the Commission capped the objection forms one person may file at 10 only on 9 October 2026. He writes that 71% of those deleted across the three phases fall under the Absent, Shifted or Others category and that many of them could be eligible to enrol again once the revision is complete, and that software flags of logical discrepancies, among them spelling differences, more than six voters linked to one ancestor and gaps of age between parent and child outside 15 to 45 years, led to the arbitrary exclusion of lakhs of eligible voters. For West Bengal he writes that more than 22 lakh appeals for inclusion had been filed and around 1.2 lakh decided by October 2026, and that of 83,000 decided by August the tribunals allowed around 75,000. He proposes a detailed audit of the final rolls, the use of the special summary revision ordered in 14 states and three union territories to enrol again those wrongly left out, and house-to-house enumeration as a requirement wherever a revision is under way, with the rolls finalised only after all claims and objections are decided.
quote: Second, the requirements of supervision of the current SIR are not as elaborate as the last SIR. The notification before Bihar’s SIR mandates 10% random verification by supervisors
However, out of more than 22 lakh appeals that have been filed for inclusion, only around 1.2 lakh had been disposed of till October 2026.
note: First reading, 23 November 2026. Read in full from the page with curl on 23 November 2026, free to read, with no isAccessibleForFree marking. The page prints November 12, 2026 under the byline, and its article:published_time is 2026-11-10T18:37:51+05:30, so the date is the printed one, as for Niraja Gopal Jayal's essay from the same site in round 51. The author line at its foot reads 'Rangarajan R. is a former IAS officer and author of Polity Simplified, a guide to the civil service exams.' and the page says the views are personal. Both quotes are verbatim. Every claim is his. Checked against data/india/states.json. His 'around 13.3 crore voters' deleted across three phases, with 2.7 crore (20%) for death, 1.01 crore (8%) as duplicates and 9.5 crore (71%) under absent, shifted or others, are close to the site's count of names left off the drafts in 31 states, 13,39,03,307, of which 2,79,69,558 dead (20.9 per cent), 1,01,48,459 duplicate (7.6 per cent) and 9,56,35,923 shifted, absent or other (71.5 per cent). His 1.01 crore matches. His 13.3 crore, 2.7 crore and 9.5 crore are each below the site's figure read to one decimal (13.4, 2.8 and 9.6), so the totals are not carried, as Jayal's 13.3 crore was not in round 51. His share of 71% under Absent, Shifted or Others is carried in his words, because it agrees with the site's 71.4 per cent. His 14 states and three union territories for the special summary revision agrees with the 17 states and union territories of the Commission's letter of 15 October in process.json. His 9 October 2026 instruction agrees with the date of the Commission's letter that process.json cites for limits on Form 7, and the cap of 10 forms is his. The West Bengal appeal counts (more than 22 lakh filed, around 1.2 lakh decided by October 2026, 83,000 decided by August of which around 75,000 allowed) are his, with no source named, and the site holds no count of appeals filed or decided to check them against. 75,000 of 83,000 is 90.4 per cent, which agrees with his more than 90%. Not carried are his statement that the revision has covered every state and union territory except Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, because process.json records that Assam was given a Special Revision in place of an intensive one, his account of the petitioners' arguments, his reading of the Manual on Electoral Rolls (2023) on notices to shifted electors, his point on the declaration attached to Form 6, his account of the Commission's later instruction on re-enrolment through the enumeration form, and his remarks on the demand to scrap the revision.
